title: II. The Old Buffoon
paragraphs: They entered the room almost at the same moment that the elder came in from his bedroom. Two monks of the hermitage were already waiting in the cell: the Father Librarian, and Father Païssy, who was said to be very learned and was in poor health, though not old. A tall young man of about twenty-two also stood in the corner, and stayed there for the whole visit. His face was broad and fresh, his narrow brown eyes clever and watchful, and his clothes were ordinary. He was a divinity student living under the monastery’s protection. His expression was one of unquestioning but self-respecting reverence. His position was dependent and beneath the guests’, so he did not bow to them.

Father Zossima was accompanied by a novice and by Alyosha. The two monks rose and greeted him with a very deep bow, touching the ground with their fingers, and then kissed his hand. The elder blessed them, then bowed to them just as low and asked for their blessing in return. The whole ceremony was carried out very seriously, with every sign of feeling, nothing like a routine rite. Miüsov, though, imagined it was all staged to impress. He was standing in front of the other visitors. He had thought it over the evening before: out of simple courtesy, since it was the custom here, he ought to step up and take the elder’s blessing, even if he skipped kissing the hand. But the moment he saw all this bowing and kissing among the monks, he changed his mind. With solemn dignity he made a rather deep, conventional bow and walked off to a chair. Fyodor Pavlovitch did the same, mimicking Miüsov like an ape. Ivan bowed with great dignity and courtesy, but he too kept his hands at his sides, while Kalganov was so confused that he did not bow at all. The elder let the hand he had raised in blessing fall, bowed to them once more, and asked them all to sit. Alyosha flushed deeply. He was ashamed. His fears were coming true.

Father Zossima sat down on a very old-fashioned mahogany sofa covered with leather. He seated his visitors in a row against the opposite wall, on four mahogany chairs upholstered in shabby black leather. The monks sat down, one by the door and one by the window. The divinity student, the novice and Alyosha remained on their feet. The cell was not large, and it looked faded. It had only the barest necessary furniture, coarse and poor. Two pots of flowers stood in the window, and there were several holy pictures in the corner. A lamp burned in front of one huge old ikon of the Virgin. Beside it hung two other holy pictures in shining frames, then carved cherubs, china eggs, an ivory Catholic cross with a Mater Dolorosa clasping it, and a few foreign engravings of great Italian artists of past centuries. Next to these expensive, artistic engravings were some very crude Russian prints of saints and martyrs, the kind sold for a few farthings at any fair. Portraits of Russian bishops, past and present, covered the other walls.

Miüsov gave all these “conventional” surroundings a brief glance, then studied the elder closely. He thought highly of his own insight. This was a forgivable weakness at fifty, an age when a clever, established man of the world can hardly avoid taking himself rather seriously. At first sight he disliked Zossima. And there really was something in the elder’s face that other people besides Miüsov might have disliked. He was small and bent, with very weak legs. He was only sixty-five but looked at least ten years older. His face was very thin, covered with a web of fine wrinkles, thickest around the eyes. The eyes were small, pale, quick and bright, like two points of light. A little gray hair showed at his temples. His pointed beard was small and sparse, and his thin lips, which often smiled, were no more than two threads. His nose was not long but sharp, like a bird’s beak.
“To judge by his looks, a spiteful soul, full of petty pride,” thought Miüsov. He was thoroughly unhappy with his situation.
A cheap little clock on the wall hurriedly struck twelve, and that got the conversation started.

“Right on the dot,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, “only my son Dmitri hasn’t shown up. I apologize for him, sacred elder!” (Alyosha shuddered all over at “sacred elder.”) “I’m always punctual myself, to the minute, remembering that punctuality is the courtesy of kings....”
“But you’re not a king, anyway,” Miüsov muttered, losing his self-control at once.

“Yes, that’s true. I’m not a king, and, would you believe it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I knew that myself. But there! I always say the wrong thing. Your reverence,” he cried, with sudden pathos, “you see before you a buffoon in earnest! I introduce myself as such. It’s an old habit, alas! And if I sometimes talk nonsense out of place, it’s with an object, the object of amusing people and making myself agreeable. One must be agreeable, mustn’t one? Seven years ago I was in a little town where I had some business, and I made friends with some merchants there. We went to the captain of police, because we had to see him about something and ask him to dine with us. He was a tall, fat, fair, sulky man, the most dangerous type in such cases. It’s their liver. I walked straight up to him, with the ease of a man of the world, you know, and said, ‘Mr. Ispravnik, be our Napravnik.’ ‘What do you mean by Napravnik?’ said he. I saw in the first half-second that it had misfired. He stood there so glum. ‘I wanted to make a joke,’ said I, ‘for everyone’s entertainment, since Mr. Napravnik is our well-known Russian orchestra conductor, and what we need for the harmony of our undertaking is someone like that.’ And I explained my comparison very reasonably, didn’t I? ‘Excuse me,’ said he, ‘I am an Ispravnik, and I don’t allow puns on my calling.’ He turned and walked away. I followed him, shouting, ‘Yes, yes, you’re an Ispravnik, not a Napravnik.’ ‘No,’ he said, ‘since you called me a Napravnik, I am one.’ And would you believe it, it ruined our business! And I’m always like that, always like that. Always hurting myself with my politeness. Once, many years ago, I said to an influential person, ‘Your wife is a ticklish lady,’ meaning it in an honorable sense, about her moral qualities, so to speak. But he asked me, ‘Why, have you tickled her?’ I thought I’d be polite, so I couldn’t help saying, ‘Yes,’ and he gave me a fine tickling on the spot. Only that happened long ago, so I’m not ashamed to tell the story. I’m always hurting myself like that.”
“You’re doing it now,” muttered Miüsov, in disgust.
Father Zossima studied the two of them in silence.

“Am I? Would you believe it, I knew that too, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, and let me tell you, I even foresaw I would, the moment I began to speak. And do you know, I foresaw too that you’d be the first to point it out. The minute I see my joke isn’t coming off, your reverence, both my cheeks feel as if they’re being dragged down to the lower jaw, and there’s almost a spasm in them. It’s been that way since I was young, when I had to make jokes for my living in noblemen’s houses. I’m an inveterate buffoon, and have been from birth, your reverence. It’s like a craze in me. I suppose it’s a devil inside me. But only a little one. A more serious one would have chosen another lodging. Though not your soul, Pyotr Alexandrovitch; you’re not a lodging worth having either. But I do believe—I believe in God, though I’ve had doubts lately. But now I sit and wait for words of wisdom. I’m like the philosopher Diderot, your reverence. Did you ever hear, most Holy Father, how Diderot went to see the Metropolitan Platon, in the time of the Empress Catherine? He walked in and said straight out, ‘There is no God.’ And the great bishop lifted his finger and answered, ‘The fool hath said in his heart there is no God.’ And Diderot fell down at his feet on the spot. ‘I believe,’ he cried, ‘and I will be christened.’ And so he was. Princess Dashkov was his godmother, and Potyomkin his godfather.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is unbearable! You know you’re lying, and that stupid story isn’t true. Why are you playing the fool?” cried Miüsov, his voice shaking.

“I’ve suspected all my life that it wasn’t true,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried with conviction. “But let me tell you the whole truth, gentlemen. Great elder! Forgive me, the last bit, about Diderot being christened, I just made up this minute. It never occurred to me before. I invented it to give the story some spice. I play the fool, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to make myself agreeable. Though sometimes I honestly don’t know myself why I do it. As for Diderot, I heard the story as far as ‘the fool hath said in his heart’ twenty times from the local gentry when I was young. I heard your aunt tell it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. To this day they all believe that the infidel Diderot came to argue about God with the Metropolitan Platon....”
Miüsov stood up, forgetting himself in his impatience. He was furious, and knew he was making himself look ridiculous.

What was happening in the cell was really incredible. For forty or fifty years, going back to the earlier elders, no visitor had come into that cell without the deepest veneration. Nearly everyone let in felt that a great favor was being done him. Many knelt through the whole visit. Many of the visitors had been men of high rank and learning, and some were even freethinkers who came out of curiosity. Yet every one of them, without exception, had shown profound reverence and tact, for here money was not in question. On one side there was only love and kindness, and on the other repentance and an eager wish to resolve some spiritual problem or crisis. So this buffoonery amazed and bewildered the onlookers, or some of them at least. The monks kept their faces unchanged and waited with earnest attention to hear what the elder would say, but looked ready to get up, like Miüsov. Alyosha stood with his head down, close to tears. Strangest of all to him was that his brother Ivan, the one person he had counted on, and the only one with enough influence over their father to stop him, now sat completely unmoved with his eyes lowered, apparently curious to see how it would end, as if it had nothing to do with him. Alyosha did not dare to look at Rakitin, the divinity student. He knew him almost intimately, and he alone in the monastery knew what Rakitin was thinking.

“Forgive me,” Miüsov began, turning to Father Zossima. “You may think I am sharing in this shameful foolery. My mistake was to assume that even a man like Fyodor Pavlovitch would know how to behave when he visits so honored a person. I never imagined I would have to apologize just for arriving in his company....”
Pyotr Alexandrovitch could say no more. Overcome with embarrassment, he was about to walk out of the room.

“Please, do not distress yourself.” The elder rose on his weak legs, took Pyotr Alexandrovitch by both hands and sat him down again. “Do not let it trouble you. I especially ask you to be my guest.” He bowed, went back to his little sofa and sat down again.
“Great elder, tell me! Does my liveliness annoy you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly. He gripped the arms of his chair with both hands, as if he meant to jump up if the answer was a bad one.

“I earnestly ask you, too, not to trouble yourself or feel uneasy,” the elder said impressively. “Do not worry. Make yourself entirely at home. And above all, do not be so ashamed of yourself, because that is the root of all of it.”

“Entirely at home? To be my natural self? Oh, that’s much too much, but I take it with grateful joy. You know, blessed Father, you’d better not invite me to be my natural self. Don’t risk it.... I won’t go so far myself. I’m warning you for your own good. As for the rest, it’s still lost in the mists of uncertainty, though there are people who’d be delighted to describe me to you. I mean that for you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. But you, holy being, I tell you, I’m simply overflowing with ecstasy.”

He got to his feet, flung up his hands and declaimed, “Blessed be the womb that bore you, and the paps that gave you suck—the paps especially. Just now you said, ‘Do not be so ashamed of yourself, for that is the root of it all.’ With that one remark you pierced me through and read me to the core. The truth is, whenever I meet people I feel I’m lower than any of them, and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, ‘Very well, let me play the buffoon in earnest. I’m not afraid of what you think, because every one of you is worse than I am.’ That’s why I’m a buffoon. It comes from shame, great elder, from shame; it’s only over-sensitiveness that makes me rowdy. If I could only be sure that everyone would take me for the kindest and wisest of men, oh, Lord, what a good man I’d be! Teacher!” Suddenly he dropped to his knees. “What must I do to gain eternal life?”
Even now it was hard to tell whether he was joking or truly moved.
Father Zossima lifted his eyes, looked at him and said with a smile:

“You have known for a long time what you must do. You have sense enough. Do not give way to drunkenness, or to loose talk, or to sensual lust, and above all, do not give way to the love of money. And close your taverns. If you cannot close them all, close at least two or three. And above all—do not lie.”
“You mean about Diderot?”

“No, not about Diderot. Above all, do not lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he cannot tell the truth in himself or around him, and so he loses all respect for himself and for others. Having no respect, he stops loving. And to keep himself occupied and distracted without love, he gives himself up to passions and coarse pleasures, and in his vices he sinks to the level of a beast. All of this comes from lying continually to other men and to himself. The man who lies to himself can be more easily offended than anyone. You know, it is sometimes very pleasant to take offense, is it not? A man may know that no one has insulted him, that he has invented the insult himself, lied and exaggerated to make it picturesque, seized on one word and made a mountain out of a molehill. He knows all this, and still he is the first to take offense. He revels in his resentment until it gives him great pleasure, and so he passes to real vindictiveness. But get up, sit down, please. All this, too, is deceitful posturing....”
“Blessed man! Give me your hand, let me kiss it.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch skipped up and planted a quick kiss on the elder’s thin hand. “It is, it is pleasant to take offense. You said that so well, I never heard it put that way before. Yes, I’ve gone through my whole life taking offense, to please myself, taking offense on esthetic grounds, because it’s not so much pleasant as distinguished sometimes to be insulted—you forgot that, great elder, it is distinguished! I’ll make a note of it. But I’ve been lying, positively lying, my whole life long, every day and every hour. Truly, I am a lie, and the father of lies. Though no, I don’t think I’m the father of lies. I’m getting my texts mixed up. Let’s say the son of lies, and that will do. Only ... my angel ... now and then I may talk about Diderot! Diderot does no harm, though a word now and then may do harm. Great elder, by the way, I was forgetting, though for two years I’ve been meaning to come here on purpose and ask you something, to find something out. Only please tell Pyotr Alexandrovitch not to interrupt me. Here is my question. Somewhere in the _Lives of the Saints_ there’s a story of a holy saint, martyred for his faith, who stood up when his head was finally cut off, picked it up, and, ‘courteously kissing it,’ walked a long way carrying it in his hands. Is that true or not, honored Father?”
“No, it is not true,” said the elder.
“Nothing of the kind appears anywhere in the lives of the saints. Which saint is the story told of, did you say?” asked the Father Librarian.

“I don’t know which saint. I don’t know, I can’t tell you. I was deceived. Someone told me the story. I heard it from him, and do you know who it was? Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov here, who got so angry just now about Diderot. He’s the one who told it.”
“I never told you that. I never speak to you at all.”

“True, you didn’t tell it to me, but you told it with me in the room. Three years ago. I mention it because that ridiculous story shook my faith, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You had no idea, but I went home with my faith shaken, and it’s been shakier and shakier ever since. Yes, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you caused a great fall. That was no Diderot!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was working himself up into a pathetic state, though by now everyone could see plainly that he was acting a part again. Still, his words stung Miüsov.

“What nonsense, it’s all nonsense,” he muttered. “I may well have told it some time ... but not to you. It was told to me. I heard it in Paris, from a Frenchman. He said it was read out at our mass from the _Lives of the Saints_ ... he was a very learned man who had made a special study of Russian statistics and had lived in Russia a long time.... I haven’t read the _Lives of the Saints_ myself, and I don’t intend to ... all sorts of things get said over dinner—and we were at dinner then.”
“Yes, you were at dinner, and so I lost my faith!” Fyodor Pavlovitch mimicked him.
“What do I care about your faith?” Miüsov was on the point of shouting, but he stopped himself abruptly and said with contempt, “You defile everything you touch.”

The elder suddenly stood up. “Excuse me, gentlemen, if I leave you for a few minutes,” he said to all his guests. “There are visitors waiting for me who came before you. But do not tell lies all the same,” he added to Fyodor Pavlovitch, with a good-humored face. He left the cell, and Alyosha and the novice hurried after him to escort him down the steps. Alyosha was out of breath. He was glad to get away, but glad too that the elder was in good humor and not offended. Father Zossima was heading for the portico to bless the people waiting there. But Fyodor Pavlovitch stubbornly stopped him at the door of the cell.

“Blessed man!” he cried, with feeling. “Let me kiss your hand once more. Yes, with you I could still talk, I could still get along. Do you think I always lie and play the fool like this? Believe me, all this time I’ve been acting this way on purpose, to put you to the test. I’ve been trying you out all along, to see whether I could get along with you. Is there room for my humility beside your pride? I’m ready to give you a certificate that a man can get along with you! But now I’ll be quiet. I’ll keep quiet the whole time. I’ll sit in a chair and hold my tongue. Now it’s your turn to speak, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You’re the main person left now—for ten minutes.”
